events.title: The trials of the Scipios
events.summary: Cato and the tribunes Quintus and Quintus Petillius demanded an account of 500 talents received from Antiochus. Africanus tore up his brother's account books in the Senate. Later, prosecuted himself, he reminded the people that it was the anniversary of Zama and led them up to the Capitol to give thanks, leaving the accusers alone. He withdrew to his villa at Liternum. Lucius Scipio was condemned to a fine; the tribune Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, though an enemy, vetoed his imprisonment.
events.detail: Livy (38.50-60) admits that his sources contradict each other hopelessly on dates, charges, tribunes and outcomes, and quotes divergent versions of Valerius Antias. The trials marked the end of Scipionic dominance and a reassertion of collective senatorial control over over-mighty individuals.
scholarship: Gruen, 'The Fall of the Scipios', in Malkin & Rubinsohn (eds.), Leaders and Masses in the Roman World (1995)
events.debate: Chronology (187 or 184) and the sequence of trials are irrecoverable; Livy himself despairs. Scullard's model of 'Scipionic' and 'Catonian' factions has been heavily criticised.

events.title: Manlius Vulso's triumph and 'the origin of foreign luxury'
events.summary: Gnaeus Manlius Vulso, after a fight in the Senate over his unauthorised Galatian war, triumphed with Asiatic booty. Livy says his army introduced to Rome bronze dining couches, costly coverlets and tapestries, one-legged tables, female lute and harp players at dinners, and cooks, who rose from the cheapest of slaves to the most valued.
events.detail: Livy (39.6.7-9), probably following Piso Frugi, dates the beginning of Roman luxury to this triumph; other moralists chose 146 (Sallust) or 133. The topos of decline through eastern wealth is itself an important Roman historiographical idea.

events.title: Via Aemilia
events.summary: The consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus built a road from Ariminum to Placentia along the foot of the Apennines, binding the newly conquered Po plain to Rome. His colleague Gaius Flaminius built a road from Bononia across the Apennines to Arretium.
events.detail: The Via Aemilia gave its name to the region (Aemilia, modern Emilia-Romagna) and fixed the line of colonies at Bononia, Mutina, Parma and Placentia.

events.title: Death of Antiochus III
events.summary: Short of money for the Apamea indemnity, Antiochus III attempted to plunder the treasury of the temple of Bel in Elymais and was killed by the local population. His son Seleucus IV succeeded.

events.title: The Bacchanalia affair
events.summary: Alerted by the courtesan Hispala Faecenia and her young lover Publius Aebutius, the consul Spurius Postumius Albinus revealed to the Senate a secret Bacchic cult accused of nocturnal orgies, forged wills and murders. A special inquiry pursued it across Italy: over 7,000 people were said to be implicated, and many were executed. The Senate's decree permitted Bacchic worship only with its permission, in groups of no more than five, with no common fund or male priests.
events.detail: Livy's lurid narrative (39.8-19) contrasts with the dry bronze copy of the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus found at Tiriolo in Bruttium in 1640 (CIL I² 581, now Vienna), addressed to the allied communities of the ager Teuranus. Interpretations range from genuine moral panic to the Senate's assertion of authority over religion throughout allied Italy (Gruen), the suppression of a cross-class, cross-gender organisation outside elite control (Pailler, North) and a pretext for intervention in allied affairs.
events.locName: Rome and Italy (copy found at Tiriolo, Calabria)
scholarship: Gruen, Studies in Greek Culture and Roman Policy (1990)
Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome (1998)
events.debate: The decree is dated to the Nones of October (7 October) 186. How far Livy's account reflects real events rather than a moralising novella, and why the Senate acted, are long debated.

events.title: First athletic contests and wild-beast hunt at Rome
events.summary: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior celebrated votive games for his Aetolian victory lasting ten days, at which Rome saw for the first time Greek athletic contests and a venatio, a hunt of lions and panthers. Many Greek actors came to honour him.

events.title: Censorship of Cato
events.summary: Cato and Lucius Valerius Flaccus held the most famous censorship in Roman history. Cato expelled seven senators, among them the ex-consul Lucius Quinctius Flamininus for killing a Gallic noble at a banquet to amuse a boy lover, took the public horse from Lucius Scipio Asiaticus, assessed luxury goods, slaves and carriages at ten times their value and taxed them, cut off private pipes illegally drawing public water, demolished buildings encroaching on public land, and let public contracts at harsh prices.
events.detail: Valerius was made princeps senatus. Cato's severity earned him a statue in the temple of Salus with an inscription praising him for restoring the Roman state when it was tottering (Plutarch, Cato 19). He also cleaned and extended the sewers. The censorship became the archetype of the censor as moral guardian.

events.title: Basilica Porcia, the first basilica in Rome
events.summary: Cato as censor bought two houses and four shops by the Curia and built the Basilica Porcia, the first known basilica in Rome, a covered hall for business and courts. The tribunes of the plebs later used it as their headquarters. It burned with the Curia in 52 BC.
events.detail: The basilica form, probably adapted from Hellenistic stoas and halls, spread rapidly: Basilica Aemilia (179), Basilica Sempronia (169) and Basilica Opimia (121).

events.title: Death of Scipio Africanus
events.summary: Scipio Africanus died in voluntary exile at his villa at Liternum, aged about 52. He reportedly asked to be buried there rather than in ungrateful Rome; Valerius Maximus quotes the epitaph 'Ingrata patria, ne ossa quidem mea habes'.
events.detail: Livy (39.52) records disagreement over the year (187 to 183) and the place of burial, noting monuments at both Liternum and the Tomb of the Scipios. Seneca visited the villa and its small dark bath (Epistles 86).
events.debate: Polybius places his death in the same year as Hannibal's and Philopoemen's (183); Valerius Antias put it earlier.

events.title: Death of Hannibal
events.summary: After Apamea Hannibal fled via Crete (where, Nepos says, he hid his treasure in amphorae filled with lead) to Armenia and then to Prusias I of Bithynia, for whom he won a naval battle against Eumenes by hurling jars of snakes onto the enemy ships. When Flamininus came as envoy and Prusias agreed to surrender him, Hannibal took poison at Libyssa, saying, according to Livy, 'let us relieve the Romans of their long anxiety'.
events.detail: Nepos (Hannibal 13) notes that Atticus dated his death to 183, Polybius to 182 and Sulpicius Blitho to 181.
events.debate: Year (183, 182 or 181) disputed in antiquity; Flamininus' role was criticised even by Romans (Plutarch).

events.title: Death of Philopoemen
events.summary: The seventy-year-old Achaean general Philopoemen, 'the last of the Greeks', was captured by rebel Messenians and forced to drink poison in prison. The young Polybius carried his funeral urn in the procession to Megalopolis.

events.title: Colonies of Parma, Mutina and Saturnia; Potentia and Pisaurum
events.summary: A burst of colonisation in the north and on the Adriatic: citizen colonies at Potentia and Pisaurum (184), Parma and Mutina with 2,000 settlers each and Saturnia (183), and Graviscae (181). Unlike earlier Latin colonies these were citizen colonies with substantial allotments.

events.title: Founding of Aquileia
events.summary: A Latin colony of 3,000 infantry families was founded at Aquileia at the head of the Adriatic to block Gallic migrations and Istrian raids; it was reinforced with 1,500 more families in 169. It was the last Latin colony founded in Italy and grew into one of the great cities of the Empire.
events.detail: Its foundation followed the expulsion of a group of 12,000 Transalpine Gauls who had tried to settle nearby in 186-183.

events.title: Discovery and burning of the 'Books of Numa'
events.summary: Workmen digging on land of the scribe Lucius Petillius at the foot of the Janiculum found two stone chests, one inscribed as the coffin of King Numa, the other containing books on pontifical law in Latin and on Pythagorean philosophy in Greek. The urban praetor judged them subversive of religion and, with the Senate's approval, burned them in the Comitium.
events.detail: The episode reflects the contemporary belief, rejected by Livy and Cicero on chronological grounds, that Numa was Pythagoras' pupil, and Roman anxiety about Greek philosophy.

events.title: Lex Cornelia Baebia de ambitu
events.summary: The consuls Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus carried the first known law against electoral bribery (ambitus), reflecting the escalating cost of competition for office. A related Lex Baebia provided for four and six praetors in alternate years, but was soon abandoned.

events.title: Lex Villia Annalis
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Villius carried a law fixing the minimum ages at which each magistracy could be held. It probably also required an interval of two years (biennium) between curule offices and made the praetorship a prerequisite for the consulship, regularising the cursus honorum.
events.detail: The law responded to the meteoric careers of the war generation (Scipio, Flamininus) and to fierce electoral competition. Under Sulla's later revision the minimum ages were 30 for the quaestorship, 39 for the praetorship and 42 for the consulship; the original Villian ages are inferred rather than attested.
scholarship: Astin, The Lex Annalis before Sulla (1958)
Evans & Kleijwegt, 'Did the Romans like Young Men?', ZPE 92 (1992)
events.debate: The exact age limits of the Villian law are not stated by any source and are reconstructed from known careers.

events.title: Pestilence and poisoning trials
events.summary: A severe epidemic struck Rome and Italy between 182 and 180, killing a consul (Gaius Calpurnius Piso), a pontifex maximus and many others. Suspicion of poisoning led to special inquiries; Livy says 3,000 were condemned in 180, among them Piso's widow Hostilia, accused of poisoning her husband to make her son consul.

events.title: Deportation of the Apuan Ligurians to Samnium
events.summary: After years of Ligurian warfare, the proconsuls Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus forcibly moved 40,000 Apuan Ligurians with their women and children to public land in Samnium, giving them 150,000 sesterces for equipment. Another 7,000 followed. The deportees formed two communities, the Ligures Baebiani and Ligures Corneliani.
events.detail: The Ligures Baebiani were still a distinct community three centuries later: a bronze alimentary table of Trajan (AD 101) found at Macchia di Circello records loans to its landowners.
events.locName: Samnium (Ligures Baebiani, Macchia di Circello) from the Apuan Alps

events.title: Battle of Aebura
events.summary: In the First Celtiberian War the praetor Quintus Fulvius Flaccus defeated a Celtiberian army near Aebura in Carpetania and in 180 fought his way through an ambush at the Manlian Pass. Livy claims 23,000 enemy killed at Aebura.

sides.strength: praetorian army under Q. Fulvius Flaccus

battle.significance: Opened the way for Gracchus' settlement.

events.title: Tiberius Gracchus' settlement of Celtiberia
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus (father of the Gracchi), praetor in Citerior 180-178, combined victories with negotiation. His treaties fixed tribute and military service obligations, settled landless Celtiberians, forbade the founding of new fortified towns, and founded Gracchurris on the upper Ebro. The peace held for 25 years.
events.detail: Polybius (25.1) mocked claims that Gracchus had taken 300 towns, saying many were mere forts. The ban on new walled towns was the legal pretext for the war with Segeda in 154.

events.title: Censorship of Lepidus and Nobilior: Basilica Aemilia and Pons Aemilius
events.summary: The censors Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Marcus Fulvius Nobilior, publicly reconciled from bitter enmity at the Senate's urging, built the Basilica Aemilia et Fulvia on the north side of the Forum, a fish market, a harbour and the piers of the first stone bridge over the Tiber, the Pons Aemilius, whose arches were completed in 142. They also reorganised voting in the tribal assembly by region, status and class.
events.detail: The Basilica, rebuilt by later Aemilii into the first century AD, preserves the family name. The voting reform (Livy 40.51.9) is obscure.

events.title: Death of Philip V; accession of Perseus
events.summary: Philip V, who had rebuilt Macedonian strength since 196, died at Amphipolis in 179, haunted, as the tradition has it, by the execution in 180 of his pro-Roman younger son Demetrius on charges brought by his elder son Perseus, supported by a letter from Flamininus later said to be forged. Perseus succeeded and renewed the treaty with Rome.
events.detail: Polybius (23.10) treats the Demetrius affair as a tragedy sent by the Furies. Roman historians portrayed Perseus as planning war from the start; modern scholars see a cautious king whose popularity in Greece alarmed Rome and Eumenes.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
events.debate: Whether the letter incriminating Demetrius was forged is uncertain.

events.title: Second Istrian War: siege of Nesactium
events.summary: After the Istrians captured a Roman camp at the Timavus in 178 (its garrison was found drunk on the captured wine when retaken), the consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher besieged Nesactium and took it by diverting the river that supplied it. King Aepulo and the defenders killed their families and themselves. Istria submitted.

sides.strength: consular army under C. Claudius Pulcher

events.title: Gracchus' war in Sardinia: 'Sardi venales'
events.summary: The consul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus crushed a rising of the Ilienses and Balari in Sardinia in 177-176, killing or capturing 80,000 according to the tablet he dedicated in the temple of Mater Matuta. So many captives were sold that 'Sardi venales' ('Sardinians for sale', i.e. cheap goods) became a proverb.
events.detail: Livy (41.28.8-10) quotes the dedicatory tablet, which bore a map of Sardinia with depictions of the battles, an early example of a Roman triumphal map.

battle.significance: Broke Sardinian resistance for a generation; flooded the slave market.

events.title: Citizen colony at Luna
events.summary: A citizen colony of 2,000 settlers was founded at Luna on land taken from the Ligurians at the mouth of the Magra; it later became famous for the white marble of the nearby Apuan quarries (Carrara).

events.title: Expulsion of two Epicurean philosophers
events.summary: In the consulship of Lucius Postumius, two Epicureans, Alcaeus and Philiscus, were expelled from Rome for corrupting the young with the doctrine of pleasure.
events.debate: The date depends on identifying the consul Postumius (173 or 155).

events.title: The Statellates affair
events.summary: The consul Marcus Popillius Laenas attacked the Ligurian Statellates, who had never fought Rome, and after they surrendered sold 10,000 of them into slavery. The Senate ordered their freedom and restitution; Popillius defied it. In 172 the tribunes passed a Lex Marcia for an inquiry, but Popillius' brother, the new consul, obstructed it and the case collapsed.

events.title: Both consuls plebeian for the first time
events.summary: Gaius Popillius Laenas and Publius Aelius Ligus were elected consuls for 172, the first time both consuls were plebeians. The Fasti Capitolini note 'ambo primi de plebe'. The Licinio-Sextian requirement that one consul be plebeian (367) had never been matched by a rule requiring a patrician.

events.title: Eumenes' denunciation of Perseus and the attack at Delphi
events.summary: Eumenes II came to Rome in person and denounced Perseus to the Senate for war preparations, his marriage alliance with the Seleucids and his intrigues in Greece. On his way home he was nearly killed by a rockfall at Delphi engineered, it was said, by Perseus' agents. The Senate decided on war.
events.detail: Livy (42.11-18) gives Eumenes' speech. Polybius (22.18) said the true causes of the war went back to Philip's resentment; modern scholars see Rome as determined to eliminate a revived Macedon regardless of Perseus' conduct.

sources.w: Roman letter to the Amphictyons on Perseus

scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
events.debate: A Roman indictment of Perseus inscribed at Delphi (Syll.³ 643) lists the official charges. The degree of Perseus' aggression is disputed.

events.title: Carteia, the first Latin colony outside Italy
events.summary: More than 4,000 men, sons of Roman soldiers and Spanish women, who as children of unions without conubium had no citizenship, petitioned the Senate for a town. They were settled at Carteia near the Strait of Gibraltar as a Latin colony 'of freedmen' (libertinorum), together with the existing inhabitants who wished to join.
events.detail: Carteia is the first Latin colony founded outside Italy and a revealing glimpse of the social consequences of long Roman service in Spain.

events.title: Spanish envoys accuse Roman governors
events.summary: Envoys from both Spanish provinces complained to the Senate of the greed of Roman magistrates. The praetor appointed panels of five senatorial recuperatores for each case, and patrons for the Spaniards, among them Cato, Aemilius Paullus and Scipio Nasica. One ex-governor was acquitted and two, Publius Furius Philus and Marcus Matienus, went into exile before verdict.
events.detail: The Senate also forbade Roman officials to fix the price of grain or to station prefects in Spanish towns to collect money. The procedure prefigured the permanent extortion court of 149.
scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

events.title: Battle of Callinicus
events.summary: Perseus caught the consul Publius Licinius Crassus' cavalry and light troops near the hill of Callinicus outside Larissa and routed them, but did not commit his phalanx to exploit the victory. He then offered peace on the terms of his father's treaty; the Romans, true to their custom of never negotiating after a defeat, refused.
events.detail: Polybius (27.8) uses the Roman refusal to illustrate a national characteristic: they were most unyielding in defeat. Greek sympathy for Perseus after the battle alarmed Rome.

sides.strength: cavalry and light infantry of P. Licinius Crassus' army
sides.losses: c. 200 cavalry and 2,000 infantry killed, 600 captured (Livy)

battle.significance: Perseus' only major victory; his failure to follow it up and Rome's refusal to negotiate set the pattern of the war.

events.title: Lex Voconia
events.summary: The tribune Quintus Voconius Saxa carried a law, supported by the elderly Cato, forbidding citizens of the first census class to institute a woman as heir and limiting legacies so that no legatee received more than the heirs.
events.detail: The law aimed to stop great fortunes passing to women; it was evaded by trusts (fideicommissa) and by not registering in the census. Cicero (Verrines 2.1.104-114) shows Verres' manipulation of it; St Augustine still found it unjust.

events.title: Marcius Philippus crosses into Pieria
events.summary: The consul Quintus Marcius Philippus led his army over a difficult pass near Lake Ascuris, lowering elephants down cliffs on ramps, and descended into Pieria behind Perseus' lines at Tempe. Perseus panicked and abandoned the passes, but recovered as Marcius' supplies failed. The Achaean cavalry commander that year, Polybius, met Marcius as an envoy.

events.title: Battle of Pydna
events.summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus faced Perseus on the plain near Pydna. On the evening before, the military tribune Gaius Sulpicius Gallus had predicted a lunar eclipse to calm the troops. Next afternoon a skirmish over a runaway pack animal at the river escalated into battle. The Macedonian phalanx advanced irresistibly at first, but as it crossed uneven ground gaps opened; Roman maniples pushed into them and the phalangites, helpless at close quarters with their long sarissas, were massacred. Perseus fled with the cavalry.
events.detail: Paullus told Polybius he had never seen anything more terrifying than the advancing phalanx (Polybius 29.17). Livy gives 20,000 Macedonian dead and 11,000 captured; Plutarch, citing Paullus' son-in-law Scipio Nasica, puts Roman losses at about 100. The battle confirmed Polybius' analysis of legion versus phalanx. At Delphi Paullus took over a pillar prepared for a statue of Perseus and topped it with his own equestrian statue; its frieze, the earliest Roman historical relief, shows the loose horse that started the battle.

battle.significance: Ended the Antigonid monarchy; Macedon was dismembered and the Hellenistic world recognised Roman supremacy.

sources.w: Monument of Aemilius Paullus at Delphi

scholarship: Kähler, Der Fries vom Reiterdenkmal des Aemilius Paullus in Delphi (1965)
events.debate: The battle date is fixed by the lunar eclipse of 21 June 168 (Julian), which Livy (44.37.8) places on 3 September by the Roman calendar, showing the civil calendar was about 2.5 months ahead of the seasons. Exact site uncertain.

events.title: Third Illyrian War: Genthius surrenders at Scodra
events.summary: Genthius, king of the Illyrians, allied with Perseus for a promised subsidy of 300 talents (mostly never paid) and imprisoned Roman envoys. The praetor Lucius Anicius Gallus defeated him in a campaign of thirty days and besieged him in Scodra, where Genthius surrendered. He was led in Anicius' triumph.

battle.significance: Ended the Ardiaean kingdom; Illyria divided into three tributary districts.

events.title: The Day of Eleusis
events.summary: Antiochus IV, having occupied much of Egypt in the Sixth Syrian War, was besieging Alexandria when the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas met him at Eleusis, a suburb of the city, and handed him the Senate's decree ordering him out of Egypt. When the king asked for time to consult, Popillius drew a circle in the sand around him with his vine staff and told him to answer before stepping out of it. Antiochus complied and withdrew from Egypt and Cyprus.
events.detail: Polybius (29.27) says Popillius acted with such confidence because news of Pydna had just arrived. The episode, famous as 'the circle of Popillius', showed that the word of a single Roman senator could now stop a Hellenistic great power in its tracks.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
events.debate: The Book of Daniel refers to the 'ships of Kittim' turning back the king of the north; Antiochus' subsequent measures in Jerusalem (167) have been linked to his humiliation.

events.title: Surrender of Perseus at Samothrace
events.summary: Perseus fled with his treasure to the sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace. Blockaded by the praetor Gnaeus Octavius' fleet and abandoned by his Cretan guards, who made off with his gold, he surrendered with his children. Paullus received him with courtesy and wept, Plutarch says, at the reversal of fortune.
